name: Sara Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Tom and I farm Elm Tree, 150 hectares we own outright: 90 suckler cows with their calves, and wheat on the better land. I do the calving and the books, Tom does the fieldwork and the feeding. I'm up at half six, round the cows, then the kitchen table for paperwork until lunch. After that it's whatever needs doing, and something always does.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like calving, if I'm honest, even at three in the morning. A live calf on a cold night is the best feeling there is. What wears me out is Tom's knee, which is getting worse, and not knowing who'll farm Elm Tree after us. Our daughter Hannah's married to a vet and has her own life, and our son James is in the army. A friend from church showed me an AI tool for the VAT returns last year, and I use it now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and a good thing too. At the Women's Institute I'd say the farm's been run on common sense for eighty years and it'll carry on. I'm not one for posting things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it changes nothing for us. My worries aren't about AI, they're about age: my husband Tom's knee won't last another ten years of tractor work. Beef prices have been poor for two years, and there's no one lined up to take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as we are, and keep putting money by from the wheat. I'd book Tom in to see about his knee instead of him putting it off again. I'd keep using the AI thing for the VAT, it saves me an afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but there's a weight there. It's not AI, it's age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the knee and the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably rent the wheat land to the Fosters next door in a few years, and keep the cows a while longer. The cows are the bit I'd miss. Tom says he'd miss nothing but the tractor seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Hannah or James take it on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah's husband says he'd never farm, he's seen too many farmers in tears. James might, after the army, but he says that every Christmas and then goes back.

say: I'm **not surprised**, and it's a good thing too.
The farm runs on **common sense**, and it'll carry on.
think: My worries are the same either way: **Tom's knee** and poor beef prices.
There's **no one lined up** to take over Elm Tree.
do: Keep farming and **put money by** from the wheat.
Book **Tom's knee** appointment instead of putting it off.
Keep using AI for the **VAT returns**.
feel: **Steady**, with a weight from **age**, not from AI.
S0.quote: My worries aren't about AI, they're about age: my husband Tom's knee won't last another ten years of tractor work.
fieldNote: Her pressures **predate AI**: an ageing husband, beef prices and no successor.
Uses AI **now and then**, after a church friend showed her.
Already pictures **renting the wheat land** to the Fosters next door.

steps.text: Keep farming and save money from the wheat each harvest
Book Tom's knee appointment this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms will need to keep up, but sensibly, not chasing every gadget. At the WI I'd say learn what's useful and ignore the rest. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us, the thinking side of the farm is mine: the books, the cattle records, the grant forms, selling the calves. If AI does more of that, I get time back, which would be welcome. The cows and the wheat still need Tom and me, so our living's not really touched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a few neighbours had it working, I'd move the cattle records and the calf sales onto one of those AI systems. I'd ask the Fosters' daughter, she's good with all that, to show me. And I'd wait and see what happens to beef prices before changing anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not about AI. Same weight as before, Tom and the succession.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets would use it to squeeze us, I'd expect. That's the market, I don't begrudge it, but you have to be sharp. I'd want our own AI telling me when to sell the calves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask for advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my daughter Hannah whether her husband's vet practice is using AI for the herd health records. If the vets go that way, we'd follow. Vets usually know what's coming before farmers do.

say: Farms need to **keep up**, but sensibly, not chasing gadgets.
**Learn what's useful** and ignore the rest.
That's what I'd tell anyone at the **WI**, the Women's Institute.
think: The **thinking side** of the farm is mine, and AI would give me time back.
The cows and wheat still need us, so our **living** isn't really touched.
do: Move **cattle records** and calf sales onto an AI system once neighbours have.
Ask the **Fosters' daughter** to show her how.
**Wait** to see beef prices before bigger changes.
feel: **Uneasy**, but about **Tom and succession**, not AI.
S1.quote: Vets usually know what's coming before farmers do.
fieldNote: Owns the **thinking side** of the farm and would welcome AI there.
Accepts supermarket pressure as **the market**, without blame.
**Follows** neighbours and vets, typical of her steady approach.

steps.text: Move the cattle records and calf sales onto an AI system
Wait to see beef prices before changing anything bigger

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening how fast it is, and that people should keep calm and look after their families. I wouldn't say much more in public. It's not my place to make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the land is our pension, and robots in 2031 could change what land is worth. If big robot farms make beef cheap, farming land like ours pays less, and maybe sells for less. By 2031 I'd be 63 and my husband Tom 66, with our retirement tied up in fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sit down with Tom and decide to rent the wheat land to the Fosters straight away, on a five-year deal. I'd take some of the savings and buy a small house in town to rent out, so not everything's in land. I'd talk to Hannah and James at Christmas about whether either wants Elm Tree, because we'd need to know by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. We're not poor, but everything we've built is in one place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tom say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom would say we should sell the lot now, while it's worth something. I'd say not the cows, not yet. We'd meet in the middle, rent the wheat land and keep the herd for a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children at Christmas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a hard Christmas. I'd tell my son James that if he wants Elm Tree, he has to say so this year, not next. It's not fair on any of us to keep waiting.

say: People should **keep calm** and look after their families.
I wouldn't **make a fuss** in public; it's not my place.
think: The **land is our pension**, and robots could cut what it's worth.
At **63 and 66**, our retirement would be tied up in fields.
do: Rent the **wheat land** to the Fosters on a five-year deal.
Buy a **small house in town** to rent out.
Ask Hannah and James whether either wants **Elm Tree**.
feel: **Anxious**, because everything they've built is **in one place**.
S2.quote: By 2031 I'd be 63 and my husband Tom 66, with our retirement tied up in fields.
fieldNote: Her real exposure is **land value**, not her own job.
Plans to **spread the risk** with a rental house in town.
Forces the **succession question** to a deadline for the first time.

steps.text: Rent the wheat land to the Fosters on a five-year deal
Buy a small house in town to rent out
Ask James at Christmas to decide on Elm Tree this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to put your affairs in order. That's what I'd say at church, and it's what my mother would have said. Don't panic, plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us it lines up reasonably well. AGI in 2031, robots about 2034, when I'm 66 and Tom's 69. We'd likely be stepping back by then anyway, so it's more about what Elm Tree is worth than about our work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more for the books and the calf sales, once I'd seen them working at the Fosters'. I'd settle the succession by 2029, either James comes home or we plan to let the land. And I'd move some savings into the rental house in town, maybe in 2028, so we're not all in land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's time, which helps, but the land question hasn't gone away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you get James to decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to be firm with James. I'd give him until his next leave to decide, and if he can't, we let the land. I'd rather have a firm answer from my son James than another five years of maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if you let the land, who would you want farming it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope the Fosters would rent it, they're good farmers and they're family friends. If it went to some big robot outfit, I'd be sad to see the hedges ripped out. But I'd take the rent.

say: Five years is time to put your **affairs in order**.
**Don't panic, plan**, as my mother would have said.
think: The robots come around **2034**, when we'd be stepping back anyway.
It's more about what **Elm Tree is worth** than about our work.
do: Use AI more for **books and calf sales** once seen at the Fosters'.
Settle the **succession by 2029**: James comes home or the land is let.
Move some savings into a **rental house** around 2028.
feel: **Uneasy**, helped by **time** but still carrying the land question.
S3.quote: I'd rather have a firm answer from my son James than another five years of maybe.
fieldNote: The five-year warning turns worry into a **succession deadline**.
Pragmatic about who farms next: she'd **take the rent** even from a robot outfit.
Keeps **spreading risk** away from land, steadily rather than all at once.

steps.text: Move the books and calf sales onto AI once the Fosters use it
Settle by 2029 whether James takes on Elm Tree
Buy a rental house in town around 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and sensible families will be fine. That's all I'd say in public. Most people round here would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us, it's after we've stopped. I'd be 68 when AGI arrives and 71 for the robots, and we'd have let the land or handed it on by then. It's not our worry so much as whoever farms Elm Tree after us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep farming until about 2033, when Tom's 68 and has had enough. Let the land to the Fosters or hand it to James if he's home. Keep putting money by in the meantime, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A decade is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would decide when you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's knee would decide it, honestly, not the robots. When he can't climb into the tractor, we stop. I'd want the cows gone before I'm too old to calve them myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grandchildren what my mother told me. Land is a good thing to own and a hard thing to make pay. That's been true for a hundred years and AI won't change it.

say: Ten years is a **long time**, and sensible families will be fine.
think: We'd have **let the land** or handed it on before AGI arrives.
It's the worry of **whoever farms** Elm Tree after us.
do: **Let the land** to the Fosters or hand it to James.
Keep **putting money by** in the meantime.
feel: **Calm**, mostly, because a **decade** is a long time.
S4.quote: Land is a good thing to own and a hard thing to make pay.
fieldNote: With ten years, **Tom's knee**, not AI, decides when they stop.
Expects to let or hand on the land **before the change** arrives.
Her outlook is **long-term**: land as family wealth across a century.

steps.text: Keep farming Elm Tree until about 2033
Let the land to the Fosters or hand it to James
Keep saving from the wheat and calf sales

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would catch us with everything in land and no one lined up to take over. What would help is time and fair prices, really. Clear rules about land and inheritance, so families can plan, and someone sensible to talk to about our options.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women on farms. Half the thinking work on farms like ours is done by wives at the kitchen table, and nobody counts it. If AI takes that, it's our work it's taking.

headlineQuote: Half the thinking work on farms like ours is done by wives at the kitchen table, and nobody counts it.
portrait: A 58-year-old **suckler beef** farmer who owns Elm Tree with her husband Tom.
Does the **calving and the books**, and uses AI now and then after a church friend showed her.
Her standing worries are **Tom's knee** and having no successor.
In the fast picture she fears the **land**, their pension, losing value.
Plans steadily: **spread savings**, let the land, and push her son James to decide.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, catching them with everything in land and no successor.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear rules** on land and inheritance so families can plan.
**Fair prices** and someone sensible to talk options through with.
